game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices. [h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3] One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored. The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes. [h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3] Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures. review_text_raw:
Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.  

Enjoy!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a classic example of doing wonders using very little. 

It won't blow you away with the graphics, but combined with the immersive, gentle soundtrack that dynamically changes as you play, and a captivating story and well written content, you'll be hooked. 

I've always very much been a fan of slower paced games that involve alot of surrounding story and Orwell provides it in droves, without being a very clumsy political statement by itself. You're dropped into the "Orwell" system and told to go to work investigating a terrorist attack, but there are no clear cut moral choices, you read the information given to you, submit what is pertinent and do your job, all the while slowly being drawn into your role as an investigator - all without a single action sequence or quicktime event. 

If atmospheric games are your thing, give it a go. The interface is clean, intuitive, the soundtrack is hauntingly beautiful, and the whole story will keep you glued to your government workstation for the duration.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is an incredible 'experience' of a game. Very immersive and gripping story right from the get go.

Characterisation is superbly done, with regular shifts in opinion of characters based on what they may or may not have done, new information comes to light constantly and you as the PC having to delicately manage your personal opinion against what is 'right' and meting out data that will in turn mete out justice.

To some of the other critics here, when looking at the gameplay elements:

There is often frustratingly insufficient evidence to go one way or the other on conflicting information - [i]That's the point[/i]. There's an allegory here for judicial systems of all stripes, that none have perfect information, even here in the information age.
And yes, sometimes you feel the need to submit certain pieces of evidence that aren't in line with the narrative you'd like to create order to progress - [i]That's the point[/i]. I felt conflicted and frustrated as a player of this [i]game[/i]. Imagine the confliction you would have in reality if you knew facts you provide would be wilfully misinterpreted by others to serve their own agenda? To be able to balance such a fine line of generating frustration in a player against the desire to see the story through to conclusion was masterful in my opinion.

A beautiful exploration of this very deep, philosophical point - that is matched by the aesthetic and depth of information to wade through in the game.

Bravo Surprise Attack Games - Orwell sets the bar in this 'cyperpunk storyteller' that will be difficult to surpass; and I'll definitely look forward to the 'datachunk' that you provide.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing. To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished my 1st playthrough, it took me about 5 hours or so.

I played in on Linux and it ran without any issue.

This is more of a Visual Novel than a game to me, so please be aware of that before being let down. There is no way to get stuck, the game always tells you what you need to click on, which is soso. There are a few choices at times, and there is also the option of not submitting some information to the system, that will alter the story somewhat.

I had a good time playing it, though at times I didn't really care about all the stuff I had to read... I still don't think I really needed to read all of it but I could be wrong. I wish there was some way to scale the text, as I play on a TV, sitting far from it. Unlike other games it's not too bad though. It feels like the whole thing should just have been in HTML/JS/CSS and allow easy scaling.

Alas, even though I started wondering about what happened and why and such, I never really cared about the characters. I find them unappealing in their own ways (mental problems, obnoxious people, etc). I never really got immersed in the story, never really felt part of it till people other than my boss start mentioning my character and by then it was too late to care.

As people have commented on the forum, even though I also assumed it was the goal, I never really got a bad feeling from the Orwell system, I think it kind of failed there, but maybe with another playthrough following some differents paths I'd feel different.

The idea of the novel and the way we play is interesting and different, that's definitely a plus, but that was pretty much all it had. Had it kept going on for 10 more episodes, I don't know if I would have finished it.

I got this game as it was suggested to me based on buying (and loving) Beholder. Between the 2 of them, I'd definitely suggest Beholder, though one is about technology not the other...

This review would a bit over neutral if I had the choice, but since I don't, it's thumbs up!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A surprisingly immersive psuedo-visual novel that plays on the tropes of governmental surveillance in a way that makes you question every action that you make in the game. The writing is absolutely try-hard sometimes, to the point of being cringey only on rare occasions, but the overall story is interesting and captivating in a way that kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through. You really begin to feel that you are an investigator, prying into the personal life of these people, and for a game so simple to do that is absolutely fantastic imo.

The mechanics are simple point, click, drag. The gameplay itself requires deducing events and character motivation through the combination of various news sources, emails, and hacked text messages. It requires a lot of reading and more thinking than I anticipated, leaving me stumped a few more times than I care to admit, but it doesn't feel boring in the slightest.

It's short, it's sweet, and it's to the point. I would recommend it to anyone that likes narrative experiences.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"[i]For how could you establish even the most obvious fact when there existed no record outside your own memory?[/i]"

Anybody who has read through George Orwell's [i]1984[/i] will recognize many prevolent themes throughout this point-and-click adventure. While many movies and games struggle to rival their literary counterparts, Orwell does a spectacular job of demonstrating the themes prevelant in George Orwell's story. While the actual story of the game is different from the book, focusing on the player rather than Winston, many of the aspects are still the same.

I only had a few minor gripes with Orwell that did not take too much away from the story or my immersion. The only real problem that I had with the game was the fact that you had to open each file up to add data to them, rather than just dragging and dropping them onto the character web.

A compelling story with many twists leaves the player hungry for more, available through multiple playthroughs of the game. A second season to Orwell would be very difficult to achieve, due to the ending of the game. I will not go into depth about what this is, as I cannot without spoiling the game.

I strongly reccomend you play through Orwell if you have read the novel [i]1984[/i] or are interested in games with themes of censorship and/or a malleable story.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.


Pros:

- Immersive gameplay and story
- Great soundtrack
- UI feels fantastic
- Great value
- Story ending felt wrapped up, not abrupt

Cons:

- Limited replayability

review_text_clean: The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be. You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online. I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation. By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop. It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm. I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours. There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig. When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation. Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools. It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling. In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong. The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly. While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted. Pros: - Immersive gameplay and story - Great soundtrack - UI feels fantastic - Great value - Story ending felt wrapped up, not abrupt Cons: - Limited replayability - 5 hours of content (I take the time to read a lot of the docs) - Not super challenging to an average player

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 312:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a tense, thought-provoking surveillance thriller that does more with a few browser tabs and text files than most games do with entire cities. It casts you as a government contractor sifting through personal data to uncover a growing threat—and forces you to wrestle with how much “truth” you really need to keep people safe. It’s slick, unsettling, and surprisingly emotional.

[b]🪬 Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Brilliant UI that doubles as storytelling. The whole game takes place inside a simulated desktop, with tabs for social media, chat logs, police records, and more. But it’s not just aesthetic! It feels like doing a job. Every click, every search result, every drag-and-drop data point creates tension. The interface is intuitive, immersive, and sinister.

[*] Deep moral ambiguity in every decision. Do you report that someone once expressed violent thoughts in a song lyric? Do you include their real name in a classified file? What about the context? The game forces you to make hard calls on limited info, and the consequences are immediate. 

[*] Tightly written and emotionally resonant. Despite being mostly text, the characters come alive through their messages, posts, and private calls. You start to see their contradictions, their fears, their humor. It’s intimate in a way that hits hard when you're the one deciding what gets flagged—and what gets buried.

[*] Great balance of investigation and puzzle-solving. The game isn’t about cracking codes or hacking firewalls: it’s about connecting dots. Who knows who? What’s fact, what’s hearsay, and what might get someone arrested? You feel clever when you catch a subtle connection between a dating profile and a news article. It’s simple but deeply satisfying.

[*] Fantastic pacing and structure. The game unfolds over five episodes, each building tension and complexity. Just when you think you know what’s going on, it flips your assumptions. It’s rare to find a game this compact that still manages to feel complete and impactful.
[/list]

👁️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Limited replay value. While your choices do have consequences, the story arc mostly funnels toward the same endpoint with slight variations. It’s a brilliant one-time experience, but it may not have the branching depth to support multiple playthroughs.

[*] Some plot twists feel a bit on-the-nose. The writing is mostly subtle, but a few characters and twists lean heavily into dystopian clichés. It's forgivable, especially for a debut game, but occasionally the nuance slips.

[*] A bit short. For players used to longer visual novels or narrative-driven games, [i]Orwell[/i] might feel more like an extended episode than a full series. That said, it’s tightly packed and doesn’t waste your time.
[/list]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw:
Review originally posted [url=https://www.backlog-assassins.net/posts/z7q2vd7/]here[/url].

9/10

This was a hell of a game. It’s one of an emerging genre of… ‘interface’ games, I guess. Like Her Story, you are literally your character in the game - what you see on screen is what your character sees, and you interact in the same way. Because of this, the game is incredibly immersive and therefore, at points, really tense!

Let me stop myself before I get too deep in here. In Orwell, you play as, ostensibly, yourself, hired as an ‘investigator’ in this new program called Orwell situated in a different country. In that country, a bomb has just exploded in a plaza, killing two and wounding a dozen or so people. Moments before the bomb went off, a woman was spotted crossing the plaza and getting on a bus. That woman had been arrested months before for assaulting a police officer in that very same plaza during a protest. Could she be connected to the bomb? Your task is to slowly collect information on her, and the people around her. What information you upload to the system cannot be taken back, and you get to choose what the narrative of what happened becomes. You can take an innocuous joke between friends and upload it, taking it out of a friendly context and giving it a sinister cast. You can shift a bias on a person by only uploading the worst of what they said, but not uploading good things about them. In this story, YOU are the faceless watcher, the cog in the wheel, that would be impeding the heroes of a more traditional story.

Holy shit, does it work.

I blasted through the game’s five chapters in one sitting, about four and a half hours on Saturday night. Nobody in this game is 100% good or bad, and there’s a lot of nuance around protesting for the ‘right’ reason in the ‘right’ way that is especially topical for me, right now, as a young woman living in an America I never really thought I’d be living in. This game doesn’t deliver any hard and fast morals at the end, it doesn’t take a definitive stance, and offers three different endings for the player to eventually pick. The game offers up a scenario and leaves it up to you to decide what you think is right… or at least, what you think is the least wrong.

The game isn’t perfect - it wears a little thin when you’re going back and achievement gathering. Like a Telltale game, once you see the constraints of the ‘world’ of the game, the illusion dissipates pretty quickly. There are a lot of real-time sections (text conversations, phone calls) that, while immersive the first time around, made me really wish I had a fast forward button for the fourth or fifth time I sat through the conversation. These are absolutely small gripes, however, and I would strongly urge anyone to pick up this game - especially while it’s still on sale.

review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is literally one of my favorite games of all time. As a point and click puzzle narrative adventure, the dystopian world it paints is really interesting. It puts you right in the seat of someone working within a government surveillance system, and the parallels to real life are chilling.

The game tackles the themes of government control and spying against there own people, in a way that feels both immersive and unsettling. You have to investigate people with almost no oversight, digging through chat logs, websites, and personal data, presented in beautifully designed 2D interfaces that feel just like the internet we use every day.

The gameplay revolves around finding and selecting highlighted bits of text. You decide which ones to submit, shaping the story as you go. This leads to multiple endings, where you can either side with the government or help those you're investigating. And, of course, there are tons of clever Easter eggs referencing the real Orwell.

It's a short but incredibly well crafted game, and I can’t recommend it enough.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Smart, subtle, and shockingly good: this one lingers long after the credits.[/h1]

Ever wondered what it would feel like to be Big Brother’s favorite intern? Orwell hands you the surveillance keys to a digital dystopia and asks: how far is too far when safety is on the line? Presented through simulated internet searches, social media sleuthing, and a stripped-down but powerful interface, this game is one of the most immersive narrative experiences I’ve played!

The choices are yours: what do you report? What gets ignored? You might think you're just dragging datachunks into files, but your decisions have real consequences, shaping a gripping narrative with multiple endings and gray-area morality at every turn. It’s as if Papers Please had a love child with 1984 and that baby learned to code.

There is a catch though : this isn't really a “puzzle” game despite the label (it’s more like an interactive spy-thriller/visual novel hybrid with branching paths and big philosophical questions). That said, I devoured it across three playthroughs to 100% the game and would gladly do more. Whether you’re a dystopia enthusiast or just looking for a smart, haunting slow burn, Orwell belongs on your must-play list, especially when it goes on sale (but even at full price, it’s a steal with around 4 hours of game play per playthrough).

P.-S. Stop reading about this masterpiece and go play it yourself. You'll thank me later for stopping you from reading too much. Going in blind is the best way to enjoy it!

About the game Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You, I can say that this game is one of the most thought provoking and immersive experiences I have had in a long time. The game takes place in a dystopian world where the government has implemented a surveillance system to monitor every aspect of its citizens' lives.

As a player, YOU are tasked with being the "investigator" who must review and analyze the information gathered by the Orwell System to uncover potential threats to society. However, it is up to you to determine what information is relevant and what is not, and every decision you make has consequences.

The game makes you feel like you have actual power over people's lives, and the experience of constantly analyzing data and making decisions about what information to act on or ignore makes the whole experience feel very intense and immersive .

The game's graphics and sound design are also excellent, bringing the world of Orwell to life in vivid detail. The characters are well developed, the dialogues captivating and thought-provoking.

Overall, Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is an excellent game that offers players a unique and immersive experience. It challenges us to think about the consequences of our actions and the ethics of surveillance in a society that values freedom and privacy. If you like narrative games that make you think, then this is definitely worth checking out.

review_text_raw:
A fun change of pace from the usual FPS/RPGs where you get to investigate and collect data on suspect individuals and possible enemies of the state! It definitely makes you feel like you're doing something worthwhile but also makes you think a bit (e.g. privacy/morality/ethics/greater good and all that jazz).

If you hadn't noticed the name is a dead giveaway as to what the game is about... George Orwell 1984. An all seeing eye. Big Brother is WATCHING you! Keeping you safe, of course.  

It's a nice, chill game that doesn't require TOO much thought - it mostly consists of dragging and dropping chunks of data to create a profile or disabling irrelevant chunks of data. You know, sometimes massive, 100+ hr long, open world RPGs are just too much in the moment and you just need something manageable and that's where this game comes in (for me anyway). 

In my opinion, it felt like there was no way to fail - choices somewhat matter and change the outcome of certain events/dialogue. I suppose there's some level of intensity at certain stages. 

There's about six chapters and the soundtrack is pretty great I think (if you like instrumental/synth/Deus Ex sounding music or whatever you call it) and each one probably lasts about 30 minutes. 

Don't ask me how I have 17 hours but I did take my time and went back for some achievements.

Based on this experience, I've added the 2nd game to my wishlist!

First played it in 2016 and got the bad ending. Decided to return to it again today and try for real this time. Completely worth it.
The story is excellent. Just when you thought you got to the bottom of it, it pulls the rug under your feet and goes even deeper. Several times i was sure i deduced everything and solved the mystery, and every time new information appeared and made me completely rethink everything. By the end it forms a messy web, yet i could see through it a coherent story and everything made sense. The whole thing is just very immersive.
Here, like in many story driven games, the gameplay is just a tool to deliver the plot, and the only thing that really matters is if it does it well without being too distracting. This may be up to personal taste, but i found it enjoyable enough that i didn't feel bored at any moment. Reading through articles and text conversations looking for useful data and following the story was engaging. Though i suppose if you don't enjoy too much reading in games it might get monotonous inbetween the story segments.
Overall would recommend it, especially if you're looking for a good engaging story.
